In [[mathematics]], a [[topological space]] (''X'', ''T'') is called '''completely uniformizable'''<ref>e. g. Willard</ref> (or '''Dieudonné complete'''<ref>Encyclopedia of Mathematics</ref>) if there exists at least one [[uniform space|complete uniformity]] that induces the topology ''T''. Some authors<ref>e. g. Arkhangel'skii (in Encyclopedia of Mathematics), who uses the term ''Dieudonné complete''</ref> additionally require ''X'' to be [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]]. Some authors have called these spaces '''topologically complete''',<ref>Kelley</ref> although that term has also been used in other meanings like ''[[completely metrizable]]'', which is a stronger property than ''completely uniformizable''.

==Properties==
* Every completely uniformizable space is [[uniformizable]] and thus [[completely regular]].
* A completely regular space ''X'' is completely uniformizable if and only if the [[fine uniformity]] on ''X'' is complete.<ref>Willard, p. 265, Ex. 39B</ref>
* Every [[regular space|regular]] [[paracompact]] space (in particular, every Hausdorff paracompact space) is completely uniformizable.<ref>Kelley, p. 208, Problem 6.L(d). Note that Kelley uses the word ''paracompact'' for regular paracompact spaces (see the definition on p. 156). As mentioned in the footnote on page 156, this includes Hausdorff paracompact spaces.</ref><ref>Note that the assumption of the space being regular or Hausdorff cannot be dropped, since every uniform space is regular and it is easy to construct finite (hence paracompact) spaces which are not regular.</ref>
* (Shirota's theorem) A completely regular Hausdorff space is [[realcompact]] if and only if it is completely uniformizable and contains no closed discrete subspace of [[measurable cardinal]]ity.<ref>Beckenstein et al., page 44</ref>

Every [[metrizable space]] is paracompact, hence completely uniformizable. As there exist metrizable spaces that are not [[completely metrizable]], complete uniformizability is a strictly weaker condition than complete metrizability.
